name: Aaron Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, governments or political parties. We don’t sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage fourteen people who coordinate suppliers for a large food packaging company, and my phone usually starts with an order somebody promised before checking capacity. I'm 43, with an MBA and high pay for the job; I use approved AI every day to compare offers, though my signature still commits the money. My wife manages a bookshop part-time, our son is eight and our daughter twelve, and we have a mortgage and 168,000 in accessible savings against monthly household spending of 7,000. There are plenty of management employers nearby, but I like building something where I am, and on Sundays I take the children out in our little sailing boat when the weather permits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful machine doesn't have to be a miracle. If our approved assistant saves a buyer half an hour comparing the same three offers, that's half an hour worth having.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel my job and our money were secure. My 8,300 take-home and my wife's 2,400 cover the 7,000 budget, including annual costs, and the 168,000 reserve isn't needed to pay ordinary bills. I'd be mildly disappointed as a person who enjoys new kit, but not disappointed about being able to plan next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the approved comparison assistant and holding the Tuesday supplier call in the first year. We'd continue the existing 3,700 monthly savings transfer and normal mortgage payment. I wouldn't buy a replacement system just because the sales pitch said ours was yesterday's technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little impatience at all the wasted announcements. A working tool and a paid invoice are enough excitement for most Tuesdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your team hear if you were disappointed by the hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I was disappointed by the talk, not by their work. My fastest buyer still catches a missing delivery charge before the software does, and I make a point of saying so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the boat spending change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd keep the existing maintenance allowance inside the 7,000 budget. It's something we can afford in this picture, rather than a new business or an investment I need to justify.

say: I'd call a **useful machine** worthwhile even when it saves only half an hour.
I'd recognise my **buyer's checking** rather than make staff carry my disappointment with the hype.
think: I consider my **job and finances** secure, with two wages covering costs and the reserve intact.
I enjoy **new equipment**, but limited progress wouldn't threaten our ability to plan a holiday.
do: Keep the **approved assistant** and Tuesday supplier calls through the first year.
Continue the existing **3,700 monthly** savings transfer, mortgage payment and budgeted boat maintenance.
S0.quote: A working tool and a paid invoice are enough excitement for most Tuesdays.
fieldNote: His **security** is supported by high pay, a household surplus and accessible savings rather than a claim that management cannot change.
He separates **consumption** from investment, explicitly calling the boat an affordable family expense in this scenario.

steps.text: Continue approved supplier comparisons and Tuesday supplier calls
Continue existing savings, mortgage payments and budgeted boat maintenance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd better turn quicker checking into fewer late orders, not just more slides about efficiency. I'd also say openly that automating planning and buying changes the number of people a department needs, including managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My role could get smaller, because comparing offers and planning supply are thinking tasks, not protected relationships. I'm confident I could compete for work locally while most people still have jobs, but I could take a pay cut or lose my current post. Having savings means I can negotiate without pretending I'm untouchable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use our assistant's already approved report function to automate my weekly supplier comparison this month, using cleared purchase records during my existing paid hours. It would produce a draft only; I'd check delivery charges and my director would retain the current approval limit for orders. In the first year I'd also arrange two conversations with local packaging employers about actual vacancies, applying only if the role and salary looked worth discussing. I wouldn't resign before a signed offer, and I'd need at least 7,000 take-home monthly to move jobs without changing our household plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the income risk and interested in making the work better. I can hold both feelings without making the team sit through a speech about courage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the report function already permitted for those records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, those purchase records are cleared for it and the function is in our present access rights. I'm changing my weekly routine, not assuming permission to put confidential supplier files into a different service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the only offer pays less than 7,000?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare a genuinely different household plan with my wife, rather than call it an acceptable offer under this one. Until we'd agreed and funded that change, I wouldn't resign for it.

say: I'd judge **quicker checking** by whether fewer orders arrive late.
I'd say **management posts** belong in the discussion when planning and buying need fewer people.
think: My **role could shrink** because supplier comparisons and supply planning are thinking tasks.
I could compete locally but risk a **pay cut** or job loss, with savings allowing less desperate negotiation.
do: Automate **weekly comparisons** using already cleared records and approved access during existing paid hours, retaining checks and current order approvals.
Discuss **local vacancies** with two employers and apply only for suitable roles and salaries.
Resign only after a **signed offer** pays at least 7,000 take-home monthly, unless we separately agree and fund a different household plan.
feel: **Anxious and interested**, seeing both personal income risk and useful improvements.
S1.quote: Having savings means I can negotiate without pretending I'm untouchable.
fieldNote: His **automation** stays within existing approval, record access and paid time, while draft output never acquires spending authority.
His **job search** separates conversations, applications and acceptance, with a pay floor unless the household agrees and funds another plan.

steps.text: Automate weekly supplier comparisons within existing approved access and paid hours
Discuss local vacancies; resign only for signed terms meeting the household pay gate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends that knowing how to manage suppliers isn't a claim on a salary if AGI can do the thinking more cheaply. I'd rather face that than spend two years polishing a title the company may no longer need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect my pay to stop around 2028, though I don't think we'd be forced into a bad decision immediately. My wife's bookshop income could also shrink when planning and customer service change, and robots around 2031 could reach more of the physical work. The reserve is real, but I don't assume the next venture would earn because I enjoyed starting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a broker's written valuation for the boat now and list it only after my wife agreed; I'd budget no proceeds until a completed sale, and stop the 450 monthly running allowance only when ownership and costs actually ended. In the first year after AGI, if my pay ended, I'd use actual cash to cover the household gap and review it monthly, counting only wages still arriving. I'd allow up to 3,000 for testing a business idea, but only from savings above a protected 84,000 reserve and after agreeing the total with my wife; I'd spend nothing until prospective customers had described an actual need. I wouldn't take employer records or assume the test produced a paying customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with enough money to be deliberate but no appetite for pretending this would be fun every day. Selling the boat would hurt my pride more than my children's school life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a business test rather than a new income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Conversations with possible customers, then a small prototype if there was something specific to test within the 3,000 cap. No invoices means no income, and an interested person isn't the same as a customer who has agreed to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your wife to work longer hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask how she saw her own work changing, not announce that she could replace my salary. Her existing wages are hers to discuss, and the budget has to work with actual agreed hours rather than the ones I'd like her to have.

say: I'd admit that **supplier management** doesn't guarantee a salary when AGI can do the thinking cheaply.
I'd rather face the risk than spend the preparation years protecting a **job title**.
think: I expect my **pay to stop** around 2028 without an immediate forced household decision.
My wife's **bookshop income** and any new venture remain uncertain, despite our real reserve.
do: Value the **boat** and list only with my wife's agreement; count proceeds and remove 450 monthly costs only after completed ownership transfer.
Draw actual **household gaps** after salary loss and review monthly, counting only wages still arriving.
Test a **business idea** only after demonstrated customer need and household agreement, capped at 3,000 above a protected 84,000 reserve.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate**, with pride attached to the boat more than to disrupting the children's school life.
S2.quote: Selling the boat would hurt my pride more than my children's school life.
fieldNote: The **boat sale** has valuation, agreement and completion gates, so neither sale proceeds nor running-cost savings are presumed.
His **venture test** has a protected reserve and loss limit without any assumed fee, client, employment protection or replacement income.

steps.text: End 450 monthly boat running costs only after completed ownership transfer and costs actually end
Test customer demand with at most 3,000 above an agreed protected 84,000 reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to look at a real set of business accounts instead of a promise of easy work. I'd rather own a small share of something I understand than pretend another management certificate defeats AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect the supplier job to end around 2031, so the extra time doesn't rescue the role. I would have more time to compare an ownership risk with living off savings. Owning machines might earn something, but customers without wages might also stop spending, and I can't ignore that just because I favour enterprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep earning now and ask the owner of the self-service laundry near the bookshop whether a minority stake was even available, without promising a purchase. If it was, I'd pay an independent accountant up to 800 from our new monthly surplus to examine three years of accounts, leases and debts before considering an investment capped at 20,000, also from new surplus while 168,000 stayed accessible. I'd buy only after my wife agreed and the written sale terms limited our loss to the stake, with no personal loan guarantee or unpaid work obligation. In the first year after AGI I'd treat any laundry income as zero until actually paid and draw household needs from cash if my job ended; automation and robots around 2034 might change that business too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the salary, but curious about an ordinary business with water bills rather than a grand promise. I'd prefer a small risk I can price to a reassuring story I can't check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner wants you to guarantee the laundry's borrowing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't buy under this plan, even if the asking price fell. The 20,000 limit means a limit on what the family could lose, not merely the first payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would owning the laundry mean working there after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not under the terms I'd consider here; I'm asking about a minority investment, not buying myself a job. Any later paid work would need a separate offer, and I'd still expect machines to change what staff do.

say: I'd examine **real business accounts** rather than buy a promise of easy work.
I'd consider **limited ownership** without pretending another management certificate defeats AGI.
think: I expect the **supplier job** to end around 2031 even with more time to prepare.
Ownership carries **demand risk**, including customers losing wages, so enterprise isn't proof of future income.
do: Enquire about a **laundry stake** and commission checks only if available, with an 800 fee cap funded from new surplus.
Buy at most **20,000** from new surplus with my wife's agreement, retaining 168,000 accessible under written terms barring guarantees and work obligations.
Count **zero laundry income** until paid and use actual cash for household needs after job loss.
feel: **Anxious and curious**, preferring a small priced risk to an unchecked promise.
S3.quote: I'd prefer a small risk I can price to a reassuring story I can't check.
fieldNote: His **investment** is conditional on availability, independent checks, written limited-loss terms and household agreement, with no purchased job assumed.
Both the **800 fee** and potential 20,000 stake use new surplus, protecting existing accessible savings and avoiding guaranteed dividends.

steps.text: Enquire about a laundry stake and fund independent checks up to 800 from new surplus
Buy only under the stated 20,000 cap, reserve protection and written limited-loss household gates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives families time to decide what matters before somebody else decides for them. I'd encourage my children to learn a skill properly, but I wouldn't pretend I could name the trade a 2039 robot couldn't touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and would still expect management pay to end, not a pension cheque to start. Our son would be eighteen and our daughter twenty-two, so promises about helping them start out could collide with our own need for income. Ten years makes me less hurried, not certain that investments or my wife's wages survive the same change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my wife now and set a ceiling of 15,000 total for helping the children with study or apprenticeships, funded only from new surplus rather than the existing 168,000 reserve. We'd discuss actual fees, living costs and the child's choice before promising any payment, with no assumption of wages during an apprenticeship. I'd continue earning and review that ceiling annually; in the first year after AGI, if my salary ended, we'd pause uncommitted gifts and recalculate against actual income and accessible savings before agreeing more. I wouldn't bring retirement forward on the strength of a ten-year investment forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the future income but less likely to hurry into a bad bargain. I'd like my children to see planning as keeping a promise small enough to honour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you direct your daughter toward a particular apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help her compare real places if she wanted that route, not decide that university was foolish or a trade was safe. A place, a wage and a qualification are three separate things to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you lower the 15,000 ceiling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lost wage or a large expense could do it before we'd committed money, and we'd tell the children directly. I won't borrow against our home to keep up the appearance that their father predicted everything correctly.

say: I'd encourage **serious skill learning** without naming a trade that robots could never reach.
I'd say the **decade** lets families decide priorities before circumstances decide for them.
think: At **53**, I expect management pay to end without a pension automatically starting.
Our children's **starting-out costs** could compete with our own income needs, and neither investments nor my wife's wages are certain.
do: Set a **15,000 total ceiling** for children's education help, using new surplus while protecting the existing 168,000 reserve.
Check **real fees**, living costs and each child's choice before commitments, without assuming apprenticeship wages.
Review annually; pause **uncommitted gifts** after any lost wage or major expense until actual income and accessible cash support commitments.
feel: **Anxious but less hurried**, wanting promises that remain affordable.
S4.quote: I'd like my children to see planning as keeping a promise small enough to honour.
fieldNote: His **education support** is a shared ceiling rather than a promise of full fees, a paid apprenticeship or an AGI-safe career.
The **ten-year horizon** changes household commitments, while he explicitly rejects assuming retirement funding from an investment forecast.

steps.text: Limit children’s education help to 15,000 total from new surplus under household review
Pause uncommitted education gifts after any wage loss or major expense pending an affordable revised budget

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because our household could lose my pay before I had tested another way of earning. I'd want honest company dates and the freedom to use my own savings for a different venture, with clear rules about what I can take from my old job. I believe markets make room for people, but I can't book a future customer on faith.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what someone is willing to sell before assuming they'll sell the house. I'd sell the boat before making the children move schools, even though the boat is the thing I bought when I finally thought we'd made it. Being able to choose the loss is still a good deal better than having no choice.

headlineQuote: I believe markets make room for people, but I can't book a future customer on faith.
portrait: Aaron is **43**, an expert MBA supplier-coordination manager with fourteen staff and high pay at a large packaging company.
He has **two children**, a part-time bookshop-manager wife, a mortgage and twenty-four months of current expenses accessible.
He uses **AI daily**, welcomes commercial risk and prefers earning and family resources to expecting public support.
His **boat and savings** provide choices, but he recognises that ownership and management experience don't guarantee demand after AGI.
biggestWorry: I fear **AGI by 2028** most because my pay could go before another way of earning is tested.
whatWouldHelp: I want **honest company dates**, freedom to use my savings and clear rules protecting my old employer's information.
